mcqs.question: A capacity forecast extrapolates only historical growth trend and ignores an upcoming product launch. What's the risk?
options: The forecast will systematically underestimate demand on the launch day, since a known one-off event isn't captured by trend or seasonality alone
None, since trend always dominates every other factor
Seasonality effects will automatically correct for the launch
Trend-only forecasts are always more accurate than ones incorporating known events
mcqs.explanation: Trend and seasonality both describe recurring patterns; a known, non-recurring event like a launch has to be added explicitly or the forecast will be wrong exactly when it matters most.

mcqs.question: Why can load testing reveal a lower breaking point than the forecasted peak assumes?
options: Load tests always underestimate real capacity due to test-environment limitations
An untested downstream dependency, such as a connection pool limit, can fail well before the raw compute capacity is exhausted
Forecasted peak numbers are always set higher than any real system could handle
Load testing only measures average load, never peak load
mcqs.explanation: Real systems have hidden bottlenecks — a connection pool, a rate limit, a downstream service — that cap throughput below the theoretical compute ceiling. Load testing surfaces exactly that gap, which forecasting alone cannot.

mcqs.question: How does an error budget make the capacity-headroom decision more concrete?
options: It removes the need for any headroom at all
It guarantees the system will never fail regardless of headroom chosen
It translates 'how much headroom' into 'how much of our allowed failure rate are we willing to spend on undercapacity' — an explicit, shared number
It applies only to application code deploys, not infrastructure capacity
mcqs.explanation: The error budget reframes a vague debate about 'enough' headroom into an explicit allocation of allowed failure — some of which you choose to spend on undercapacity risk versus other failure causes.

mcqs.question: A service averages 1,000 req/s across the day but spikes to 5,000 req/s during a 20-minute lunch rush. Sizing capacity from the daily average would:
options: Correctly handle the lunch rush, since averages already account for spikes
Only affect cost, never the system's ability to stay up
Have no effect on reliability, since averages and peaks always align
Leave the system undercapacity during the exact window traffic matters most
mcqs.explanation: Averaging smooths out the spike entirely, so a plan built on the average would provision for roughly a fifth of the actual peak — undercapacity precisely when the SLO is most at risk.

mcqs.question: A team forecasts a stable floor of 40 instances and a variable peak up to 120. Which pricing approach best matches that forecast?
options: Reserve/commit all 120 instances to get the maximum possible discount
Reserve or commit to roughly the 40-instance floor, and cover the variable portion up to 120 with on-demand or spot capacity
Run everything on-demand, since committed pricing never applies to variable workloads
Reserve none of it and rely entirely on spot instances for both floor and peak
mcqs.explanation: Committed pricing pays off only for capacity that's actually used continuously -- that's the floor, not the peak. Committing to the full peak overpays for capacity that isn't always needed, while avoiding commitment entirely forfeits real, certain savings on the floor.

mcqs.question: Two regions are each provisioned for exactly their own forecasted peak traffic. Why might this capacity plan still fail during an incident?
options: It correctly handles growth, but leaves no headroom for one region to absorb the other's traffic if that region fails over during an outage
This is always sufficient capacity planning as long as growth forecasting was accurate
The only fix is adding a third region with no other changes
This scenario is exclusively a networking/DNS problem, unrelated to capacity
mcqs.explanation: Growth-only capacity planning says nothing about failover -- if a sibling region's traffic has nowhere to land, the plan was never sized for that scenario. The fix is N+1 headroom sized for absorbing a neighbor's failover load, not just adding another region without addressing the same gap.
